title: the departure
hook: bark clothes are brought out, Sita doesn't know how to put them on, and Lakshmana's mother gives him one verse
carry: think of the forest as Ayodhya

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure began with gifts, and an old man's staff flying across the river. Today, the goodbyes, and the end of a week.

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk to the palace on foot. Crowds line the streets, and Valmiki lets us hear them: people who cheered for the coronation this morning are weeping now, and some openly criticize the king. Inside, the whole family is waiting: the old king, the queens, counselors, priests. This is the last room before the road. And someone has brought a pile of clothes made of tree bark.
screen: `THEY WALK TO THE PALACE.` → `THE CROWDS WEEP.` → `A PILE OF BARK CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha begs Rama, one last time, to stay just one night. Rama gently refuses. The king orders the army and the treasury to go with him; Kaikeyi objects, and Rama himself turns it down. Why keep the rope, he asks, once you've given away the elephant? Then Kaikeyi hands out the bark garments. Rama and Lakshmana trade their fine clothes for them. Sita takes one and stands holding it, confused. She has never worn anything like it. She doesn't know how to tie it, tries, can't, is ashamed, and starts to cry. Rama ties it for her, over her silk. Vasishtha, watching, finally loses his temper with Kaikeyi. Sita was never part of the boons, he says. She doesn't need to wear bark. And the king orders clothes and jewels for Sita, enough for all fourteen years. Then the mothers speak. Kausalya counsels Sita. And Sumitra gives her son Lakshmana one verse: rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi māṃ viddhi janakātmajām, ayodhyām aṭavīṃ viddhi, gaccha tāta yathāsukham. Think of Rama as your father Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya. Go, my son, and go happily. This week, Sita argued and won. Lakshmana raged, held back, and took up a spade. Gifts were given. And now a mother sends her son into exile by telling him he isn't leaving home at all.
screen: `STAY ONE NIGHT. NO.` · `SITA CAN'T TIE THE BARK.` · `VASISHTHA: SITA WASN'T IN THE BOONS.` · `SUMITRA: THE FOREST IS AYODHYA.` · then, large: `RĀMAṂ DAŚARATHAṂ VIDDHI.`

segments.voice: Try Sumitra's words on wherever you are. On a breath in, notice this room, this chair, this light; on a breath out, let it be home, nothing to escape, nothing missing. If your mind drifts somewhere you'd rather be, gently bring it back, and call this home again.
The departure, part two: the goodbyes. Bark clothes, Rama tying Sita's, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya.
Your line: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Next week, the road. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.

howItsDone: Sumitra's verse, rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi, is recited and taught as a picture of how love can make any place home.

fork.setup: you're Sumitra. your son is leaving for fourteen years in the forest with his brother. what do you tell him?
options: come back as soon as you can.
think of Rama as your father, Sita as me, the forest as Ayodhya.
fork.reveal: her verse tells him he isn't leaving home: home goes with him.

original.note: Sanskrit valkala: bark, and clothing made of bark, worn by forest ascetics.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sumitra just says goodbye.
what it means: she tells Lakshmana that Rama is his father, Sita his mother and the forest his home.
what a scholar hears: some commentators also read the verse a second way, with Rama as Vishnu and Sita as Lakshmi, so that the forest becomes heaven itself.

chat.says: What did Lakshmana's mom tell him when he left for the forest?
options: Think of Rama as your father, Sita as me, and the forest as Ayodhya. Go happily.
Come back as soon as you can, and bring Rama home before Bharata is crowned.
Don't go; your place is here with me and the old king in Ayodhya.
chat.meaning: Sumitra's verse sends Lakshmana off: Rama as his father, Sita as his mother, the forest as Ayodhya. Go, and go happily.

Vasishtha.meaning: the royal family's priest and teacher
